title: Explicit near-optimal vertex expanders
formal: Is the following proposition true? For every rational \(\delta>0\), there exists an integer \(d_0\ge3\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge d_0\), there exist a rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), real \(K>0\), integer \(a\ge1\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) which, for every integer \(j\ge1\) supplied in unary, outputs a finite simple undirected \(d\)-regular graph \(G_j\) within \(K(j+1)^a\) bit operations, with strictly increasing vertex counts \(n_j=|V(G_j)|\), and such that \[|\Gamma_{G_j}(S)\setminus S|\ \ge\ (d-2-\delta)|S|\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V(G_j)\text{ with }1\le |S|\le\eta n_j?\]
why: Random regular graphs have almost the largest possible external neighborhood for every small set. Matching that additive guarantee by deterministic constructions would sharpen a central benchmark for expanders, with consequences for combinatorial structures underlying coding, routing and pseudorandomness.
status_note: Uncertain after individual review on 2026-09-16. The original Open Problem 10.8 states the sharp additive external-neighbor bound d-2-delta. The 2025 lossless-expander paper cites that historical problem while its displayed main theorem establishes arbitrarily small fixed relative loss at sufficiently large degree. The review did not verify a theorem meeting the literal additive target and quantifier order. This card therefore neither claims the target resolved nor certifies its continued openness.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

category_assignment.reason: The main demand is an explicit expander construction with a sharp small-set vertex-expansion guarantee.

Its central graph-theoretic target and broad connections justify high importance; current open status of the exact sharp form remains separately uncertain.

sentences: The goal is to construct arbitrarily large regular graphs by a deterministic polynomial-time procedure.
Every sufficiently small set must have almost the largest possible number of distinct neighbors outside itself.
The original survey asks for the sharp additive expansion factor of the degree minus two minus any fixed positive tolerance.
The 2025 lossless-expander breakthrough gives an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss, with a degree threshold depending on that loss.
Because these quantified guarantees differ, the precise original target is retained with uncertain current status rather than being marked solved from the relative theorem alone.

definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or multiple edges. It is \(d\)-regular if each vertex has exactly \(d\) distinct neighbors. Its labeled vertex set is \([n_j]=\{1,\ldots,n_j\}\). For \(S\subseteq[n_j]\), define
\[
\Gamma_{G_j}(S)=\{v\in[n_j]:\ \exists u\in S,\ \{u,v\}\in E(G_j)\}.
\]
The left side in the target counts distinct neighbors outside \(S\), not edges leaving \(S\), not neighbors counted with multiplicity, and not neighbors inside \(S\). The cutoff \(\eta n_j\) is a real number; the condition is imposed on every integer set size satisfying the displayed inequality. Empty sets impose no requirement. The same positive \(\eta\) works for the entire family at the fixed values of \(\delta,d\).

The output of \(A\) is \(n_j\) in binary followed by an explicit list of the edges, each an unordered pair of distinct binary vertex labels, with delimiters. Isolated vertices would still be specified by \(n_j\), although none occur for \(d\ge3\). Reading the unary index, all computation and every output bit count in the bound. The machine has a finite program, no random bits, advice, oracle or uncharged preprocessing. It must work on every \(1^j\), not merely on infinitely many selected indices. The integers \(n_j\) must increase strictly, so the construction gives arbitrarily large graphs; an allowed family need not contain every admissible vertex count.

The degree threshold \(d_0\) may depend on \(\delta\). After \(d\) is fixed, the machine \(A\) and constants \(\eta,K,a\) may depend on both \(\delta,d\), but not on \(j\) or \(S\). No algorithm uniform in \(\delta,d\) is required. The construction requirement is the survey's mild explicitness convention, polynomial time in the family index, with full output charged. It does not additionally require computing one neighbor in time polynomial in \(\log n_j\). Restricting positive \(\delta\) and the small-set fraction to rationals loses no expansion guarantee: a smaller positive rational tolerance or fraction can be chosen when needed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the entire proposition, including the explicit algorithm families, their cost bounds and the expansion inequality for all indicated sets, or a complete Lean proof of its negation. Random existence alone is insufficient. A construction with a relative loss tending to zero as degree grows does not meet this additive-loss target without a proof of the displayed bound with the stated quantifier order. A result for one degree or a one-sided bipartite expansion promise does not by itself establish the proposition.

context_blocks.text: The saved survey explicitly asks for \(d-2-\delta\) external vertex expansion for every sufficiently large degree, with a positive small-set fraction depending on \(d,\delta\). This card preserves that additive target. Definitions 2.3 and 4.6 supply the mild explicitness and external-neighborhood conventions; it does not replace the question by a relative \((1-\varepsilon)d\) target.

Theorem 4.16 shows that random regular graphs have the displayed small-set expansion asymptotically. This establishes the combinatorial feasibility of the bound, not a deterministic polynomial-time family.

Hsieh, Lubotzky, Mohanty, Reiner and Zhang give explicit lossless expanders: for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), all sufficiently large degrees admit a \((1-\varepsilon)d\) distinct-neighbor guarantee. Their introduction cites the survey question as a longstanding problem addressed by their construction.

The two quantitative formulations are not identical. A degree threshold depending on \(\varepsilon\) does not by itself justify taking \(\varepsilon\) proportional to \(1/d\) at the same degree. Moreover, counting all distinct neighbors and counting only external neighbors differ. The review therefore does not infer the exact additive \(d-2-\delta\) proposition from the stated relative-loss theorem.

The retained status is uncertain because the limited review has not established the present status of this sharper literal survey formulation after the lossless-expander breakthrough. The formulation is precise, and the original source question is preserved; the uncertainty concerns current resolution, not a license to claim the broader historical problem remains unsolved.

Psi_V counts Gamma(S) minus S, and the target is additive d-2-delta for every sufficiently large degree.

Read the cached full Hsieh–Lubotzky–Mohanty–Reiner–Zhang 2025 paper introduction, Theorem 1 and Theorem 2.2; its complete construction proof had also been examined for the distinct relative-loss card TCS-1009. Theorem 1 has fixed epsilon followed by a sufficiently large degree threshold d0(epsilon).

Quantifier audit: substituting epsilon=(1+delta)/d is not justified by an unspecified d0(epsilon); the desired degree may fail d>=d0((1+delta)/d). An all-neighbor lower bound loses up to |S| when converted to external neighbors. Therefore the displayed relative theorem alone does not establish the sharp additive original statement.

The later introduction explicitly cites HLW Open Problem 10.8 as a longstanding problem addressed by its result. This tension is disclosed in the card and leads to uncertain status, not a claim that the authors proved or failed to prove a different theorem.

Bounded follow-up searches through 2026-09-16 included 2025 lossless constructions and the September 2026 unbalanced two-sided-expander result. No inspected theorem established the exact external additive guarantee. This does not certify that the sharp form remains open.

Kept the source’s mild explicitness branch with unary family index and polynomial full-output time. Did not add a polylogarithmic neighbor-query requirement, require every vertex count, restrict to Cayley graphs, or discard the card merely because of the current-status ambiguity.
